newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hamas denies links to alleged bombing plot in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Hamas denies links to alleged bombing plot in U.S..

text.p: The militant Islamic resistance movement Hamas denied on Saturday that it had any connection to an alleged New York subway suicide bombing plot.

U.S. law enforcement sources on Friday linked suspects in the alleged conspiracy to Hamas and officials said disaster was only hours away when police seized five pipe bombs and arrested three men on Thursday in a raid on a Brooklyn apartment.

"We deny any connection between us and the prisoners or the accusations against them. Hamas does not consider the American people an enemy and it does not target any of its communities," Hamas said in a leaflet faxed to international news agencies.

Two of the three men arrested, Gazi Ibrahim Abu Mezer, 23, and Lafi Khalil, 22, were shot and wounded in the raid and were charged in hospital on Friday with conspiracy to blow up a subway and possession of explosives.
The law enforcement sources said investigators had evidence that the suspects made telephone calls to the Hamas organisation from stores near the apartment.
A joint FBI and New York City police statement alleged that the suspects intended to target "U.S. and Jewish interests worldwide."

The Hamas leaflet said the movement had repeatedly stated its rejection of attacks against targets other than Israel. "Hamas targets only the Zionist occupation by its Jihad (holy war) and its battlefield is Palestine," the leaflet said.

A leaflet issued on Wednesday in the name of Hamas claimed responsibility for a twin suicide bombing in Jerusalem's main Jewish market that killed 15 people, including the two attackers, earlier that day.
Israeli officials say they are not certain it is authentic.

The head of the FBI in New York, James Kallstrom, declined to comment on any possible links between the suspects and Hamas. President Bill Clinton has also said it is too early to draw conclusions about the case.

A New York attorney for Moussa Abu Marzook, leader of the political wing of Hamas, said on Friday that his client called the suspects "cowboys" who were probably upset by the conditions of the Palestinian people.
"It's absolutely absurd," Stanley Cohen quoted Marzook as saying from Jordan, where he was deported in May after being held without trial for two years in a U.S. prison.
"It's ridiculous and a total lie that Hamas had anything to do with these guys wanting to plant pipe bombs."
